solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Jump start (6)

blocks.note: to begin or arise suddenly, as water rises from a source

annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two meanings of one verb: SPRING can mean a leap and also a beginning, as when an idea springs up.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for the leap, while the start sense comes from a spring as a source where things begin.

entries.clue: Position leader of Sunday Times defends (6,2)

indicatorNotes.leader of: the leader of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a stand is a position, as in 'take a stand'
times = by, as in six by four

annotation.surface: A notice about where the Sunday Times editorial puts its lead story, or who it champions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sunday Times' looks like the newspaper's own name, but it splits in two: the S from Sunday and multiplication's BY.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand by someone is to defend or support them.

entries.clue: Fight fire in carrier at the back (8)

blocks.note: a ruck is a scuffle or brawl
to fire someone is to sack them

annotation.surface: A soldier fighting a blaze from inside a vehicle's rear compartment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fire' suggests flames, but it is the dismissal sense. A ruck is also a rugby scrum-like tussle, a sport widely played in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: the bag is worn strapped to the shoulders, so it carries its load behind the walker.

entries.clue: Dramatist, after casting she rejected Bottom (5)

indicatorNotes.casting: casting a play rearranges its parts among actors, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.rejected: SHE is thrown out of the dramatist's name

blocks.note: Richard Brinsley Sheridan, author of The School for Scandal

annotation.surface: A dramatist whose leading lady turned down the part of Bottom in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
annotation.walkthrough: Bottom is Shakespeare's weaver, which pulls the reader toward the theatre; here it just means the lowest point.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the astronomical term for the point directly underfoot has come to mean any lowest point.

entries.clue: Combat medal on medic’s clothes (8)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, the medal comes on (after) the medic

blocks.note: OBE = Order of the British Empire, a British honour

annotation.surface: A battlefield decoration pinned to a doctor's uniform.
annotation.walkthrough: The OBE is a British honour conferred by the monarch; crosswords treat it as a stock 'medal' or 'award'.
annotation.definitionFit: Metonymy: the cupboard's name passes to the garments it holds, as in 'a new summer wardrobe'.

entries.clue: Emerges outside leading hotel with a new playwright (12)

indicatorNotes.outside: ARISES sits outside the other pieces

blocks.note: H = hotel in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A dramatist stepping out of a top hotel with a newcomer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leading hotel' reads as one phrase, a grand hotel; it splits into TOP and H.
annotation.definitionFit: Aristophanes was the great comic playwright of ancient Athens.

entries.clue: A pin I held, altering bloomers (9)

indicatorNotes.altering: the letters are altered into a new order

annotation.surface: A seamstress holding a pin while taking in a pair of old-fashioned knickers.
annotation.walkthrough: Bloomers are baggy women's underwear, and alterations with a pin fit that picture; here a bloomer is simply something that blooms, a flower.
annotation.definitionFit: Delphinia (delphiniums) are flowering plants, things that bloom.

entries.clue: Tear rising to men’s eyes? (6)

indicatorNotes.rising: in a down clue, rising means read upwards

annotation.surface: A tear welling up in a man's eye.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all about crying, but 'tear' is a rip, a snag. The question mark flags that eyes are just one example of organs.
annotation.definitionFit: Eyes are organs of the body; the question mark signals a definition by example.

entries.clue: Natural oils, perhaps, bottled in what year? (6)

indicatorNotes.bottled in: ART is held inside EH like liquid in a bottle

blocks.note: oil paintings are an example of art

annotation.surface: A shopper asking which vintage some bottled natural oils are.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oils' looks like cooking or essential oils in the natural-products picture; it means oil paintings.
annotation.definitionFit: Earthy means natural, unrefined, down to earth.

entries.clue: Picked up chest relief in shopping mall (6)

indicatorNotes.Picked up: picked up by the ear, i.e. heard

annotation.surface: Someone collecting a chest-pain remedy at the shopping centre pharmacy.
annotation.walkthrough: An ark is an old word for a chest or box, as in the Ark of the Covenant.
annotation.definitionFit: An arcade is a covered row of shops.

entries.clue: Countryman, fifty, into sex and booze (8)

indicatorNotes.into: L goes into the join of VI and LAGER

blocks.note: sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals
lager is a type of beer

annotation.surface: A middle-aged rustic with a taste for the pleasures of the flesh and the bottle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sex' is the Latin number six, so VI; the surface makes it the other thing entirely.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the rural sense of countryman, a man living in the countryside rather than a fellow citizen.

entries.clue: Best nuts but not the ultimate biscuit (5,7)

blocks.note: CRACKERS (nuts, mad) without its last letter

annotation.surface: A snack review: the finest nuts, though not the very last word in biscuits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like a food on the biscuit plate; it means crazy. A cream cracker is a plain, crisp British savoury biscuit, eaten with cheese.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by genus: it is a specific brand-style item in the British biscuit tin, where crackers count as biscuits.

entries.clue: Abandon sailor, going back for soldier (6,3)

indicatorNotes.going back: something going back travels in the opposite direction, so the sailor's letters are read from the end

annotation.surface: A navy deserter returning to swap places with an army man.
annotation.walkthrough: The Desert Rats were the British 7th Armoured Division, famous for the North Africa campaign in the Second World War.
annotation.definitionFit: A Desert Rat is a soldier of the British 7th Armoured Division.

entries.clue: Feeling round the back (5)

blocks.note: a noun: an intuition, a sense that something is so
a verb phrase: to curve the spine forward, bending the shoulders

annotation.surface: Someone groping around behind something in the dark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' is a verb here, to make round, not a preposition; 'feeling' is a noun, not groping.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for the intuition, and a verb for the posture; the two senses are unrelated.

entries.clue: Champions drinking in hearty congratulations (12)

blocks.note: to champion someone is to back them
lapping = drinking, as a cat laps milk

annotation.surface: Winners toasting their success with drinks all round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Champions' looks like the noun, winners; it is the verb, supports.
annotation.definitionFit: The literal gesture of slapping someone's back has become the idiom for effusive, often self-congratulatory praise.

entries.clue: This Ringo hit captured a spirit (5,4)

annotation.surface: A Beatles single that caught a ghost, or took a drinker's fancy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hit' pretends to be a chart hit by Ringo Starr, the Beatles' drummer; it is what he struck with his sticks.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: Ringo Starr was the Beatles' drummer, and 'hit' is a past participle, the thing he struck.

entries.clue: Small amount of stone to flog to church (8)

blocks.note: a pit is a fruit stone
to tan someone's hide is to beat them

annotation.surface: Someone selling a little bit of stone to a church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flog' in the surface means to sell; here it means to beat, as in tanning a hide.
annotation.definitionFit: A pittance is a very small amount, usually of money.

entries.clue: Dances start off just with records (3-5)

annotation.surface: A DJ opening a dance evening simply by spinning records.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only'; it means fair, honest. The one-step was a quick ballroom dance of the early 20th century.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by genus: an early-1900s ragtime ballroom dance with one step per beat, pluralised to match.

entries.clue: Drunken support a foreigner announced (12)

indicatorNotes.announced: what is announced is spoken, so heard

annotation.surface: A tipsy endorsement of an outsider, made publicly.
annotation.walkthrough: Bacchus was the Roman god of wine, whose rowdy festivals give the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Bacchanalian means marked by drunken revelry.

entries.clue: Coming out with aphorisms (6)

annotation.definitionNote: adjectival phrase: gnomic = full of aphorisms

indicatorNotes.out: letters that are out of order, knocked out of place

annotation.surface: Someone who emerges spouting wise sayings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coming out' reads as a single phrase meaning emerging; it splits into fodder and indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Gnomic speech is made up of gnomes, short pithy maxims.

entries.clue: Swimwear for large chests (6)

blocks.note: a trunk is a large storage chest

annotation.surface: Swimming shorts sold for muscular, broad-chested men.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chests' suggests torsos to go with the swimwear; it means storage boxes.
annotation.definitionFit: Trunks are both men's swimming shorts and big luggage chests.

entries.clue: Daring presumption (5)

annotation.surface: A bold assumption.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are close: nerve as bravery, and nerve as cheek ('of all the nerve!').
annotation.definitionFit: Nerve means both courage and impudent presumption.

entries.clue: Stories one’s acted out (9)

indicatorNotes.out: letters knocked out of their order

annotation.surface: Tales that someone performs rather than merely tells.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Acted out' looks like one phrasal verb; 'acted' belongs to the fodder and 'out' alone is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Anecdotes are short stories told about real events.

entries.clue: Poet’s dull ode stripped back (5)

indicatorNotes.stripped: ODE is stripped of its outer letters

blocks.note: ODE without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A critic dismissing a poet's tedious ode as bare and backward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a reversal instruction; it is simply REAR. 'Poet's' marks DREAR as a literary word for dreary.
annotation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic form of dreary, meaning dull.

entries.clue: Plant an explorer found on an island (8)

indicatorNotes.found on: in an across clue, DRAKE is placed on (after) MAN

blocks.note: the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

annotation.surface: A botanist-explorer discovering a new species on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man lies between Britain and Ireland; MAN is crossword shorthand for it.
annotation.definitionFit: The mandrake is a plant with a forked root, famed in folklore.

entries.clue: A scene about meeting with ghosts? (6)

annotation.definition: A scene about meeting with ghosts?
annotation.surface: A film scene in which characters encounter spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a seance is a scene about meeting ghosts, and its letters are A SCENE rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A seance is a meeting held to contact the spirits of the dead.

entries.clue: Cloth cape remains simple (8)

blocks.note: ash is what remains after burning

annotation.surface: A plain cloak made of what's left of some fabric.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cape' is a garment in the surface, next to 'cloth'; here it is the map abbreviation C.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by genus: fine goat-wool fabric named after Kashmir, where the goats were first raised for it.

entries.clue: Advocates underwear (6)

blocks.note: a brief is slang for a barrister or lawyer

annotation.surface: Lawyers in their undergarments.
annotation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'brief' is a lawyer, from the brief of instructions a barrister receives.
annotation.definitionFit: Briefs are lawyers in slang and also a kind of underpants.
